Breaking: Why U.S. Soccer's move to name Emma Hayes to the USMNT hiring committee makes sense

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, WASHINGTON, D.C.
  • women's national team head coach, will also have a say in the matter.
  • In a recent development, men's and women's national teams rarely overlap at any given federation, largely because there's little need for a crossover event.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, WASHINGTON, D.C. – By the time U.S. Soccer confirmed Mauricio Pochettino's departure for Manchester United early Friday morning, the announcement itself was far from a surprise. The press release included the usual formalities – Steve Cherundolo, the U-23 U.S. men's national team head coach, would fill in for the Dec. 13 friendly against Jamaica that falls outside the FIFA international match calendar, and the assurance that the search for Pochettino's USMNT successor would begin shortly. Federation CEO J.T. Batson and COO Dan Helfrich will unsurprisingly lead the search, as will "the soccer leadership team at U.S. Soccer that includes" assistant sporting director Oguchi Onyewu. There was one unique detail tucked into the announcement, though.

Emma Hayes, the U.S. women's national team head coach, will also have a say in the matter.

In a recent development, men's and women's national teams rarely overlap at any given federation, largely because there's little need for a crossover event. They operate on different calendars and in the best case scenarios, each team has dedicated members of staff. Hayes' name-drop as news of Pochettino's exit became official, then, is a unicorn-like sighting, even if U.S. Soccer often champions a spirit of collaboration between all of its national teams. It is uncommon for the head coach of one senior national team to help recruit a counterpart but in U.S. Soccer's case, it makes complete sense.

Hayes' coaching career, which spans two decades and two continents, means her inclusion on the federation's soccer leadership team is an obvious one. She is amongst the most respected soccer minds in the game, which easily makes her one of the most crucial people on U.S. Soccer's payroll no matter how you look at it. That will be especially true in a hiring process that has to conclude with a compelling follow-up act to Pochettino's splashy arrival two years ago. Her perspective might actually be vital in the process, which only adds to the intrigue of what's next for the USMNT.

"We have an extraordinary gift, which is a women's national team manager who's incredibly insightful, bright mind about the sport, who has a set of personal experiences and relationships that span the club and international game, the men's and women's game, the domestic and international club game, and who also has lived in the shoes of what it's like to be a U.S. national team senior coach," Helfrich told CBS Sports on Thursday. "It is a no-brainer that that mind and that voice has a really prominent seat at the table when we're talking about key moves for the federation.".

USMNT coaches are rarely style hires; look no further than the list of people to hold the job on a full-time basis this century and the picture paints itself. The only thing Bruce Arena, Bob Bradley, Jurgen Klinsmann, Gregg Berhalter and Pochettino seem to have in common, outside of the job they all once held, is that they were all tasked with some sort of cultural reset depending on the task at hand. That likely will not be the case for Pochettino's successor, though, who will inherit a team with a clear style of play, a healthy mix of veteran players and rising talents and plenty of time on the clock until the next World Cup. The job will be defined in part by continuity, even with the necessary allowance for the latest hire to put their unique spin on things.

Recent findings suggest that that's where Hayes' expertise should play a crucial role, and the same goes for Onyewu. Hayes' tactical know-how makes her as qualified as anyone employed by U.S. Soccer to establish the right stylistic profile for the next USMNT coach, especially with the spirit of continuity in mind. Pochettino's track record with the U.S. team was mixed but at its best, his high-intensity, attack-minded approach suited the player pool really well and continues to do so. Hayes, a tactical pragmatist who prioritized attack-minded teams herself with Chelsea and the USWNT, will be more than able to help match candidates to the player pool they will spend the next several years working with. Hayes admitted as much on Wednesday when addressing the topic for the first time.

"I work really closely with J.T. in particular and even more so with Dan as we're growing to develop the American soccer movement and J.T. asked if I would be involved as a technical voice, to be involved with the process and I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men's national team coach," she stated. "My role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job, albeit with the women's team, and that I've coached for a number of years and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why and like I said, I feel confident in the group that are being put together. I think it'll be a very thorough process. I think that's the most notable part of it and like I said, I feel very embedded in what we're doing with the federation so it doesn't feel unusual to me so, like I've said many times, let's build off the good work that Mauricio has done. I think that's the important part and let's get it right.".

It has been revealed that that's especially true considering the fact that there are very few slam-dunk candidates to replace Pochettino. Pep Guardiola, months into a sabbatical after a decade with Manchester City, is an obvious target for U.S. Soccer but it is entirely unclear how interested he would be in the vacancy. If he's out of the running, the list of contenders with genuine international appeal dwindles rapidly but it does not necessarily mean the list of worthy candidates vanishes with Guardiola. The hiring committee will need to be strategic in that case, both in terms of creating a list of contenders and then narrowing them down over the interview process, Hayes providing an important perspective along the way.

The jobs of the USMNT and the USWNT head coaches are hardly apples-to-apples but even then, one will still have an acute idea of what the other's job entails. There is inherent value in having a coach help in the process of hiring another coach, since they hold such singular positions – they are often treated as the be-all, end-all when it comes to their team's success, fairly or otherwise. She can also speak to the cadence of national teams, which varies greatly from the club game where coaches essentially work with their players every day during a long season.

Recent findings suggest that "Everyone is aware of the major differences between coaching at the club level and international level, and the main difference is just time on the field and time with your players," Hayes told CBS Sports earlier this year when asked about Pochettino. "Every international coach would love to have more time with their team, but that's not the nature of the international calendar and it's something I know we both had to get used to and are still getting used to … I mentioned a few times that it's almost like we are grandparents. We get to see the players for a week or so and then we send them back to their parents, which is their clubs.".

Sources indicate that outside of her tactical expertise, though, Hayes represents U.S. Soccer's ambitious turn in recent years as much as Pochettino does. She was hired because of her reputation as a serial winner at Chelsea, where she won eight league titles and seven cups. She continued the trend in short order with the USWNT – two months after officially starting in the role, she won Olympic gold at the Paris Games in 2024. U.S. Soccer has equally ambitious goals for the men's team, though the timeline will understandably be longer for that program. They continue to target the USMNT's first World Cup quarterfinal appearance since 2002 but in between, they also hope to medal in the Olympics' men's soccer event, which is contested by U-23 teams, for the first time when the Games come to Los Angeles in 2028. More than many at the federation, Hayes has experience with the intangibles it takes to reach those heights and that's exactly why she was hired in the first place. It also reflects what U.S. Soccer's executives are looking for in the next USMNT head coach.

"The most important characteristic is someone with ambition that matches ours, which is high and so when you have, then, that high shared ambition, then you look for the experience, the talent, the understanding that accompanies that ambition," Helfrich said.

Beyond that, though, Hayes in particular has an idea of what the USMNT job might entail. She is the best of both worlds – she began her coaching career in the U.S. two decades ago and has a deep understanding of the American soccer landscape, but made a name for herself in her native England and can also bring a useful outsider's perspective. There is no perfect equivalent to Hayes waiting for the USMNT job since no coach with experience in the American game has truly broken into the top tiers of the sport just yet, the federation likely to settle for one or the other. Hayes' understanding of both orbits, though, makes her an important guiding force along the way. She might be the only qualified person to answer how much to weigh the insider's perspective with the accomplished outsider's point of view when looking for the next USMNT head coach, in large part because she is the only person who boasts an equal share of it.

Recent findings suggest that hayes' expertise alone means she will be as valuable a sounding board as any, to the point that it's hard to minimize her ability to offer input down to one or two straightforward things. There is one more thing Hayes might have that no one at U.S. Soccer does – easy access to some of the most notable coaches in the game.

Over the course of her successful 12-year tenure at Chelsea, Hayes became one of the most respected coaches in England. She became the first woman to win the Football Writers Association's Tribute Award in 2024 shortly before leaving England for the U.S., and has earned the praise of many of her counterparts in the men's game along the way. Out of anyone at U.S. Soccer, Hayes might actually have the most compelling list of phone numbers in her contacts. She has said Sir Alex Ferguson, a coaching legend if there ever was one after his storied 27-year tenure at Manchester United, calls her "from time to time." Hayes has been in touch with a handful of her contemporaries over the years, including those who have been on U.S. Soccer's radar at one point or another. In her 2024 book, "A Completely Different Game," Hayes said she heard from Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp after having an emergency hysterectomy because of endometriosis in 2022. The pair "sent me long messages, expressing deeply felt emotions," as did Graham Potter and David Moyes.

The rolodex is a covetable one, if ex-U.S. Soccer sporting director Matt Crocker can serve as an example. His greatest accomplishments during his three-year spell, which came to an end in April when he took a similar role with the Saudi Arabian Football Federation, were hiring Hayes and Pochettino. He had previously worked with Pochettino at Southampton a decade earlier, which made U.S. Soccer's approach easier when discussions started. Hayes' value exceeds her ability to hand her bosses a phone number but it is unlikely to go unnoticed at U.S. Soccer, who clearly understands the expertise she would bring to the search in a variety of ways.

NWSL introduces new player development rule to incentivize youth investment, aims for further expansion

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The biggest week on the NWSL calendar is here as the buildup towards the 2026 NWSL Championship is underway.
  • According to recent reports, this year, the commissioner welcomed media to the NWSL Championship in Washington, D.C., and celebrated record ticket sales, attendance, and future expansion ahead of Saturday night's championship between the Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current, live on CBS at 8 p.m.
  • Recent findings suggest that the commissioner introduced the new player development rule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest week on the NWSL calendar is here as the buildup towards the 2026 NWSL Championship is underway. An awards show, countless events, and media days were all on the agenda ahead of Saturday's significant game. That included the annual state of the league by commissioner Jessica Berman on Thursday.

According to recent reports, this year, the commissioner welcomed media to the NWSL Championship in Washington, D.C., and celebrated record ticket sales, attendance, and future expansion ahead of Saturday night's championship between the Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current, live on CBS at 8 p.m. ET. She also revealed a few upcoming league rules and future match events.

Here are the latest things coming to NWSL:.

Recent findings suggest that the commissioner introduced the new player development rule. While the league previously submitted paperwork for a potential future second=division league, conversation and planning around that is at the moment paused with the upcoming 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and efforts to grow NWSL in other ways.

"As we grow from 16 to 18 teams in 2028, we know that we have to prioritize the pipeline, not just the pipeline of players, but the pipeline of talent that supports the players in the daily training environment. One of the things that makes the United States so uniquely positioned in the global women's soccer landscape is the depth of that potential pipeline," remarked Berman in her opening remarks.

Industry observers note that "That's why today we're announcing the NWSL Player Development Rule. It's an crucial step in strengthening the pathway to professional soccer for the next generation of players. The rule creates actual incentives for clubs to invest in identifying, developing, and retaining young talent, and it gives the clubs the flexibility to design their programs in the way that makes sense with their sporting philosophies.".

More information and the types of incentives will roll out for clubs as the upcoming player development rule goes into effect, but it is another step in future roster-building for clubs now alongside general player signings, transfers, the High Impact Player rule, and the Under-18 mechanism.

Sources indicate that the addition of the rule is paving the way for more support staff and systems in place. The commissioner also announced the new NWSL Sporting Executive Program, meant to provide more support for club leadership development. The inaugural set of leadership includes six executives from the league who will participate in the program.

"Developing the future of the sport is not just limited to the players; it's also about the technical staff who surround those players each and every day ... this is a first-of-its-kind program invested in talent, and it was curated and developed in collaboration with U.S. Soccer and FIFA. This newly introduced year-long initiative will provide sporting executives at our clubs with curated, specialized education, mentorship, and leadership development opportunities tailored around the unique demands of our league and the women's professional game," she mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that the NWSL commissioner then announced the future site of the next NWSL Challenge Cup. The 2027 NWSL Challenge Cup will take place in Austin, Texas, next summer.

According to recent reports, the tournament has evolved since its first iteration as a placeholder for the COVID-19-affected season and is now a unique one-off marquee match between top clubs, typically the NWSL Shield titleholders and the NWSL Championship winners. In years where one club wins both, the game is a rematch of the previous NWSL Championship match.

"Following the success of this year's Challenge Cup in Columbus, where we took the event to a neutral site to give an opportunity to introduce the NWSL to a latest community," she said.

The 2026 NWSL Challenge Cup was between 2025 NWSL Shield winners Kansas City Current and 2025 NWSL Championship winners Gotham FC. The 2026 competition was held in Columbus, Ohio. The state will now welcome its first NWSL franchise in 2028 alongside another expansion club in Atlanta.

Fans will undoubtedly make the connection and wonder if there is a future where an NWSL club calls Austin home. Currently, there are three NWSL clubs in California and only one in Texas, the Houston Dash.

"We're really excited to create another special experience for our fans and our players while making the NWSL a place that can invite upcoming audiences," Berman noted about heading to Austin.

In a recent development, commissioner Berman celebrated the league's recent return to the nation's capital for another NWSL Championship. The city hosted the 2022 event and now returns four years later with more attention on the league, the clubs, and its players than ever before.

It has been revealed that "Today, we're bigger, stronger, more visible, and more ambitious than ever before, and the next five years are going to redefine what's possible. We have an extraordinary opportunity in front of us, and we intend to seize it," she said.

Two incoming clubs set for 2028 and latest player roster rules are just the beginning of NWSL's next chapter. There's still the potential for more clubs on the horizon, and current clubs Houston Dash and Racing Louisville are in the process of vetting for a sale to new ownership as franchise entry fees into the league are booming to new heights.

And of course, there is still the biggest game of the year to play on Saturday.

Industry observers note that "The Washington Spirit are back in the championship for the third consecutive year, determined to bring home that title. And standing in their way is the Kansas City Current, with its own ambitions to win a championship after winning the Shield in 2025. These are two exceptional clubs, two incredibly passionate fan base, and the championship is still to be decided, [we're] very excited about the rest of this week.".

#220434. No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal

No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a fresh draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.
  • The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
  • This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating challenges such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a fresh draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.

The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.

This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating challenges such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.

The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey.

It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.

Industry observers note that the draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, stated negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.

Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.

"This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he noted in a statement.

According to recent reports, another hotly contested concern at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.

Sources indicate that the second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries. It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world.".

"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," said Raman.

The European Union has said it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.

The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.

It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.".

Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand.".

The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.

The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries stated the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community.".

The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.

Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.

On Thursday, Panama noted it would block any agreement that does not meet its demands for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate methane.

The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, stated Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.

Australian Energy Minister Bowen stated he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.

"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a plan we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming.".

The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.

The conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.

Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such as Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.

"It's critically crucial for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," stated David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Aerial scenery of Hengqin Free Trade Zone, China.
  • Two-thirds of the world’s population will be living in cities by 2050, according to the latest estimates by the United Nations.
  • Some cities are embracing these technological advances at a much faster pace than others.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aerial scenery of Hengqin Free Trade Zone, China. Credit: Weiming Xie/Shutterstock.

Two-thirds of the world’s population will be living in cities by 2050, according to the latest estimates by the United Nations. Coinciding with the mass movement of people into urban areas is the rapid integration of technology into many of those spaces. From automated subterranean waste-collection systems to driverless vehicle zones, these ‘smart-city’ solutions are changing the way that people live, work and move through their environments.

Some cities are embracing these technological advances at a much faster pace than others. Places such as Beijing, Helsinki, London and Singapore stand out for the way they are integrating smart-city technology into existing infrastructure and services.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

According to recent reports, other cities are emerging with these technologies integral to their operations from their inception. But as the examples of Songdo in South Korea and Hengqin in China illustrate, building smart infrastructure from scratch is only half the challenge: these places must also attract and retain the research and innovation talent needed to develop, operate and improve it. It’s a ‘chicken-and-egg’ problem, claims Songdo-based urban-planning researcher, Dakota McCarty: talent follows world-class universities and thriving economic zones, which need a critical mass of expertise and investment to be attractive.
